Summary
Data source overview: The paper introduces “Scientific Regret Minimization” (SRM), an iterative workflow that combines a highly-predictive but opaque neural network with an interpretable psychological choice model to analyse 40 M human moral-dilemma judgements (“Moral Machine”). It shows that (1) classical statistical model-selection fails on very large datasets, (2) raw residuals are noise-dominated, and (3) smoothed residuals obtained from the neural network reveal systematic errors (“axes of difference”) which, once included as new deontological features, greatly improve the transparent model and are confirmed in preregistered experiments.

Inference strategy justification: All risks, intermediate reasoning steps (model-selection limits, residual properties, identification of latent features, iterative refinement) and interventions spelled out by the authors were mapped. Two minor, clearly-flagged, AI-safety–oriented inferences were added (lifecycle & maturity ratings).

Extraction completeness explanation: Every clause that links the top-level risk (“misinterpreting drivers of moral judgements”) to the concrete actions proposed (run SRM; add axes features; run confirmation experiments) is represented. Nodes are sized for seamless merging (≈16 nodes ≈15 / 5000 w).

Key limitations: The source focuses on social-science methodology; transfer to AI safety needs future cross-source linking. Confidence and maturity levels are approximate because only one case study is available.

EXTRACTION CONFIDENCE[86]

How to improve instruction set: Allow an explicit “method” intervention type so that iterative modelling frameworks like SRM can be split into smaller action steps without violating the “no outgoing edges from intervention nodes” rule; clarify handling of meta-scientific validation interventions.
